paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 5, Work, Energy and Power: work and the work-energy theorem
paragraphs.key_phrase: work is force times displacement along it
paragraphs.meaning: Work is force times the displacement along it, so a force at right angles does none. Drag a 10 kg crate 5 m with a 50 N pull at 30 degrees and you do about 217 J, but if friction takes 20 N over that distance the net work is only about 117 J. The work-energy theorem then gives the speed directly: the crate reaches roughly 4.8 m/s from rest.

words.meaning: Force times displacement times the cosine of the angle between them.
words.breakdown: W = Fd cos θ. A 50 N pull at 30 degrees over 5 m gives 217 J.
words.trap: Work can be negative. Friction does negative work on a sliding crate, which is why it removes kinetic energy.

words.meaning: The net work on a body equals its change in kinetic energy.
words.breakdown: W net = ½mv² - ½mu², and it holds even when the force varies.
words.trap: The theorem uses net work. Counting only your pull and not friction overstates the final speed.

words.meaning: A force whose size changes with position, so work is the area under its graph.
words.breakdown: W is the area under the force-displacement curve.
words.trap: Fd only works for a constant force. For a varying one, use the area or an average force.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M30 116h260M30 116V30'/><path class='d-fill' d='M30 116h150v-24H30Z'/><path class='d-accent' d='M30 116c90 0 120-10 150-42'/><rect class='d-line' x='70' y='86' width='56' height='30' rx='2'/><path class='d-accent' d='M130 100h34M154 92l10 8-10 8'/><text class='d-label' x='34' y='26'>F</text><text class='d-label' x='196' y='120'>x</text><text class='d-label' x='176' y='74'>area is the work</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A force-displacement curve with the area under it shaded and labelled as the work done.
paragraphs.hook: Push a wall all day and you have done nothing, as far as the wall is concerned.
paragraphs.exam_note: Most questions give a force-displacement graph and ask for a speed. The area gives the work, and the theorem gives the speed.
paragraphs.trap: Work uses the component of force along the displacement. Multiplying the full force by distance overcounts.

recall.q: A crate is dragged 5 m by a 50 N force at 30 degrees. The work done by that force is about
recall.why: W is Fd cos θ, which is 50 times 5 times 0.866, about 217 J.

recall.q: A 10 kg crate gains 117 J of kinetic energy from rest. Its speed is about
recall.why: Energy is ½mv², so v is the square root of 2 times 117 divided by 10, about 4.8 m/s.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the worked values against your copy.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 5, Work, Energy and Power: potential energy and conservative forces
paragraphs.key_phrase: path does not matter for conservative forces
paragraphs.meaning: A conservative force does work that depends only on the endpoints, which is what allows a potential energy to exist. Compressing a 200 N/m spring by 0.1 m stores 1 J, and releasing it against a 0.2 kg block gives the block about 3.2 m/s. Gravity qualifies as conservative; friction does not, because a longer route burns more energy.

words.meaning: A force whose work around any closed path is zero.
words.breakdown: Gravity and spring force are conservative; friction and drag are not.
words.trap: A constant force is not automatically conservative. Friction is constant and still dissipates energy.

words.meaning: Energy stored in the arrangement of a system because of a conservative force.
words.breakdown: Spring: ½kx², which is 1 J for 200 N/m and 0.1 m. Near the Earth: mgh.
words.trap: The zero of potential energy is a choice, so negative values are normal. Only differences affect motion.

words.meaning: The sum of kinetic and potential energy.
words.breakdown: It is constant when only conservative forces act.
words.trap: Mechanical energy is not conserved when friction acts, though total energy always is.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M24 122h272'/><path class='d-accent' d='M60 122c0-56 40-56 40 0'/><path class='d-muted' d='M60 122c30-30 90-30 120 0'/><circle class='d-fill' cx='100' cy='72' r='5'/><text class='d-label' x='112' y='54'>same height,</text><text class='d-label' x='112' y='70'>any route</text><text class='d-label' x='188' y='112'>the hump costs nothing extra</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: Two routes between the same heights, showing equal work for a conservative force.
paragraphs.hook: Climb to the first floor by the stairs or the lift: gravity charges the same fare.
paragraphs.exam_note: Spring questions set ½kx² equal to ½mv². Incline questions use mgh and ignore the path length.
paragraphs.trap: The spring constant is force per unit extension, in newtons per metre, not newtons.

recall.q: A spring of constant 200 N/m is compressed by 0.1 m. The energy stored is
recall.why: Energy is ½kx², which is 0.5 times 200 times 0.01, giving 1 J.

recall.q: The work done by a conservative force around a closed loop is
recall.why: Start and end coincide, so no net work is done, which is the defining property.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 5, Work, Energy and Power: power
paragraphs.key_phrase: power is how fast work is done
paragraphs.meaning: Power is the rate of doing work, and for a body moving under a force it is Fv. Lifting 200 kg of water 15 m in 60 s needs about 500 W of useful power, and a pump that is 70 percent efficient draws about 714 W to do it. Energy is billed in kilowatt hours, where one kilowatt hour is 3.6 million joules.

words.meaning: The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred.
words.breakdown: P = W/t, and P = Fv when force and velocity are along the same line.
words.trap: Power is not energy. A low power motor can do a large amount of work if it runs long enough.

words.breakdown: 1 kW is 1000 W. A kilowatt hour is energy, not power.
words.trap: A kilowatt hour is 3.6 million joules. Treating it as a unit of power is a common slip.

words.meaning: Useful output energy divided by total input energy.
words.breakdown: A 70 percent efficient pump needs more input power than its useful output.
words.trap: Efficiency cannot exceed 100 percent, so a value above one means the inputs were mixed up.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><rect class='d-line' x='30' y='40' width='80' height='56' rx='2'/><path class='d-accent' d='M118 68h24M134 60l10 8-10 8'/><rect class='d-line' x='190' y='58' width='80' height='20' rx='2'/><text class='d-label' x='34' y='112'>same work, slow</text><text class='d-label' x='190' y='112'>same work, fast</text><text class='d-label' x='190' y='46'>more power</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: The same work done slowly and quickly, with the faster one labelled as more power.
paragraphs.hook: Work is the fare. Power is how fast you paid it.
paragraphs.exam_note: Constant speed up a slope means the applied force balances the weight component plus friction, and power is that force times the speed.
paragraphs.trap: At constant speed the net force is zero, but the applied force is not. Power uses the applied force.

recall.q: A pump lifts 200 kg of water 15 m in 60 s. Its useful power is about
recall.why: The work is mgh, about 200 times 10 times 15, which is 30 000 J, and dividing by 60 s gives 500 W.

recall.q: A pump with 500 W of useful output at 70 percent efficiency draws
recall.why: Input equals useful output divided by efficiency, so 500 divided by 0.7 is about 714 W.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the worked values against your copy.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 5, Work, Energy and Power: collisions
paragraphs.meaning: Momentum is conserved in every collision because the forces are internal to the pair. Kinetic energy survives only in an elastic collision; in a perfectly inelastic one the bodies stick together and the difference becomes heat and sound. A 2 kg body at 3 m/s hitting a stationary 4 kg body and sticking gives 1 m/s, and 6 of the original 9 J disappear.

words.meaning: A collision in which kinetic energy is conserved.
words.breakdown: Equal masses in a head-on elastic collision simply exchange velocities.
words.trap: Elastic does not mean the bodies separate gently. It means no kinetic energy is converted.

words.meaning: A collision in which the bodies stick together and share one velocity.
words.breakdown: It loses the maximum possible kinetic energy while conserving momentum.
words.trap: The lost energy does not vanish. It becomes deformation, heat and sound.

words.meaning: The ratio of separation speed to approach speed.
words.breakdown: e = 1 for elastic, e = 0 for perfectly inelastic, in between for real collisions.
words.trap: A ball that rebounds to 0.64 m after a 1 m drop has e = 0.8, and momentum was still conserved with the floor.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M20 116h280'/><circle class='d-line' cx='80' cy='96' r='16'/><circle class='d-line' cx='140' cy='96' r='16'/><path class='d-accent' d='M96 96h28M118 88l10 8-10 8'/><circle class='d-line' cx='220' cy='96' r='16'/><circle class='d-line' cx='248' cy='96' r='16'/><text class='d-label' x='56' y='136'>before</text><text class='d-label' x='200' y='136'>stuck, slower</text><text class='d-label' x='196' y='56'>energy lost</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: Two masses approaching, then moving together more slowly after a perfectly inelastic collision.
paragraphs.hook: Momentum balances the books in every collision. Kinetic energy does not.
paragraphs.exam_note: A bullet embedding in a block is the standard case: momentum before equals momentum after, and energy comes afterwards.
paragraphs.trap: Never conserve energy through an inelastic collision. Use momentum first, then energy for whatever happens next.

recall.q: A 2 kg body at 3 m/s sticks to a stationary 4 kg body. Their common speed is
recall.why: Momentum is 6 kg m/s before and the combined mass is 6 kg, so the speed is 1 m/s.

recall.q: In that collision, the kinetic energy lost is
recall.why: Before, the energy is 9 J; after, it is ½ times 6 times 1 squared, which is 3 J, leaving 6 J lost.
